public_rationale: Marcus said chatbot-linked delusions were a growing problem. 'Apparently' hedges on cause, so the test is whether documented cases were rising before January 2026. They were. A peer-reviewed Danish study of about 54,000 psychiatric patients, covering records up to June 2025, found a clear rise over time in notes describing harmful chatbot use. Worsened delusions were the most common harm. In December 2025, the WSJ reported that top psychiatrists had seen dozens of such cases in the prior nine months. The study's lead author says part of the rise reflects more awareness among staff. He also says the problem is likely under-counted. The evidence supports the claim as worded.
limitations: The evidence covers documented cases, not true incidence. Awareness may inflate the trend.
Causation is not established, but the claim itself hedges with 'apparently'.
The Danish data end in June 2025, and the full study was published after the post.

our_interpretation: Plain reading: in the period up to January 2026, documented cases in which chatbot use was linked to delusions were becoming more frequent.
'Apparently' is read as hedging on causation, not on the trend. So causation does not have to be proven. A rise in documented cases is enough.
criteria.support_condition: Clinical, research, or news evidence that documented cases of chatbot-associated delusions rose over 2025 up to January 2026.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence that documented cases of chatbot-associated delusions were flat or falling before January 2026, or that reports of a rise were found baseless.
